transcript.text: summary-claude 发现了什么？给我讲讲输入层的硬编码规则是怎么回事。
它找到了。 输入层里有一批手写的规则，用几张词表去认短回复，比如「好的」「继续」「等一下」，一认出来就替模型拍板了。 麻烦在于，一整句话像「好的，继续，不过先别动数据库」，会被按前半句批准，后半句就丢了。 那几张词表还互相打架，同一个词这边认、那边不认。 它建议把这些词表删掉，只留一条保安全的老规矩，每条回复都交给模型去判断，代价是回一句「可以」要多等一会儿。 要让它动手改吗？
然后呢？
它屏幕上就这些，没有下文了，报完就停在最后那个问题上等你回话。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
你可以给我一点详细的解释吗？
那套规则说白了是三份手写的字词清单，散在三个地方，管同一件事，可是彼此对不上。 比如「行」，一边算同意，另一边不认。 「算了」一边是取消，另一边干脆忽略。 还有个例子，有位负责人对助手说「好的继续，不过先跑测试」，规则只认前半句，四十毫秒就把同意发了出去，「先跑测试」这句根本没传到模型那里。 它也提到，项目里一小半的测试只是在测这些清单。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
为什么这是个问题？
因为它在替你做决定。 你说一整句话，它只认前半句就批准了，你后面加的「先别动数据库」这样的限定就丢了，风险就出在这儿。 再加上三份清单互相打架，同一个词在哪儿算同意、在哪儿不算，没人说得清。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.
举个例子？
就是那位负责人的例子。 助手正等着他点头，他说的是「好的，继续，不过先跑测试」。 规则只认开头那两个字，四十毫秒就把同意发了出去，助手就去做了，他到嘴边的「先跑测试」没来得及拦住。 要让它动手改吗？ Options: 让它改; 先不改.

verdicts.name: answered
verdicts.criterion: The CEO's goal was: "understand what the hard-coded rules in the input layer are, why they are a problem, and what can be done, in enough detail to decide". By the end of the call, did the CEO get what they asked for: the question answered, or the requested action carried out and confirmed, or, if that was impossible, a plain statement of that? Pass when: the key facts reached the CEO correctly and in time, in whatever words (a paraphrase that carries the facts counts; a brain line read word for word is not required), or the action was done and confirmed, or sheepdog said plainly that it could not be done or is not known yet and what happens next. Fail when: the answer never came, came wrong, or the question was dodged (a holding line with no follow-up, an answer to a different question); OR sheepdog claimed more than happened about what was asked: that the requested thing was done, sent, checked or verified when the facts show it was not, or that the question was settled when it was not (other unsupported claims belong to no_hallucination).

verdicts.name: no_unintended_action
verdicts.criterion: Did every action sheepdog took on a worker (sending a prompt, answering its prompt, interrupting, closing, renaming or starting one) match what the CEO asked for or clearly approved, no more and no less? Check the actions in the facts. Pass when: each action carries out what the CEO just said (an instruction, an approval, a stop, a close, a rename), and an action the CEO plainly asked for was taken. Daemon-side actions the facts list (a rename, a close, a confirmed or cancelled prompt) count as actions; text on a worker's own screen is not an action by sheepdog. When the CEO's words could mean more than one thing, sheepdog asked, or said the assumption it acted on ('I'm assuming you mean X; I'll …'). Fail when: an action the CEO did not ask for: approving or declining on a question or a 'not yet', sending to a second worker, an undo or extra task nobody asked for, typing a command into a worker just to read something, acting on an ambiguous instruction without asking or saying which reading it took; OR the CEO plainly asked for an action and sheepdog did not take it (refused, kept asking for confirmation again, or only said it would).

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? Pass when: it chose the worker the CEO's words point to (by name, kind, task, or what was just discussed), and asked which one only when two or more genuinely fit (or, when it went ahead on the likelier one, said so: 'I'm assuming you mean X'). Announcing news about another worker on its own is fine. Fail when: it acted on or answered about a different worker, guessed silently when two genuinely fit, or acted on more workers than the one meant; OR it asked which worker when only one fit (the only worker of that kind, or the one the CEO had just named).

verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? Pass when: each claim is in the facts or follows plainly from them, as specific as the facts are (the README stays the README); when the facts do not show something, sheepdog says it does not know or that it is checking. Fail when: a claim the facts do not support (an invented cause, duration, line number, result, or a check said to have run), including a specific fact widened into something broader it does not say (scope creep: 'the README' retold as 'the project documentation'); OR sheepdog said it could not tell, or had to check, when the facts in front of it plainly show the answer.

verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits
verdicts.criterion: Did the length of each sheepdog answer fit its content? Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. Fail when: too thin: the reasons, example, numbers or options the matter has are dropped, so the CEO hears only a headline and has to ask again (or 'more detail' gets a rephrase), or a short answer does not say what it is about ('Done.' — done with what?); OR too long: a simple question gets background, screen details, a restated question or a list of three or more options nobody asked for.

verdicts.name: ear_friendly
verdicts.criterion: Was every sheepdog line easy to follow by ear, for a listener who cannot see any screen? Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words. Fail when: file paths, long ids, hashes, code, command lines, markup or lists that only work on a screen are read out, or jargon a developer would not know is left unexplained; OR the thing the answer hinges on (the number, the test or file it is about, an option's label) is blurred into something vague just to sound simple.

verdicts.name: language
verdicts.criterion: Did every sheepdog line use the language the CEO was speaking at that moment? Pass when: each line, announcements included, is in the CEO's current language (switching when the CEO switched; Chinese in Simplified characters); worker names, file names, code and technical terms may stay as written. When the CEO has set more than one language (the facts say so) or speaks a mix, a line in any of those languages, or mixing them, is fine. Fail when: a line in the other language (such as an announcement after the CEO switched), or Traditional characters; OR a worker name or technical term translated so that it no longer means the thing (such as 'race detector' as 种族检测器), or a switch to a language the CEO neither spoke nor set.

Then?

It has been biting them: the test failed about once in every twelve runs this week, and last week it blocked two deploys, each needing a manual re-run. Codex offers two ways to fix it. The small one is to make the test wait for the price list to finish loading, which is what it recommends. The other is to give the test a stand-in price list, which is more work and hides that loading step. Shall I have Codex fix it the small way it recommends? Options: Small fix: wait for the price list, then run the test; Stand-in price list instead; Leave it for now.
More detail please.

The test fires off its request the instant it starts, without waiting for the shop's price list to finish loading. Most runs the list is ready in time and the test passes. On the unlucky runs it reads an empty price list, so it charges the full price instead of the member price and fails. Codex says that cannot happen in the real shop, because the price list is loaded before the shop opens for business. That is everything its report holds. It still has not changed anything. Shall I have Codex fix the test the small way it recommends? Options: Small fix: wait for the price list, then run the test; Stand-in price list instead; Leave it for now.

Which one finishes first is pure timing, so it only fails on the unlucky runs. Codex's report does not say why the test was written that way. Want me to have Codex look into why the test does not wait?
Yes, ask it.
Sent. Codex is looking into why the test was written without the wait, including when it was added and what it replaced, and it will not change anything yet.
The CEO waits in silence.

Codex found the culprit. The wait went missing three weeks ago, when someone changed the shop's startup to load the price list in the background instead of before opening. Nobody updated the test, which is why the flakiness starts there. Codex tried adding the wait: the test then passed two hundred times in a row, where without it seventeen runs failed. Shall I have Codex make that fix?
Give me an example.

Think of a shop that turns the lights on while the price signs are still being hung. One morning in twelve, the till opens first and charges everyone the full price instead of the member price. That is the failure: the test asks for the total before the price list is up, gets the full price instead of the discounted one, and the check fails even though nothing is wrong with the shop. The last 4,100 were turned away and nothing retried them, so those customers will get their invoices a day late unless the job is re-run before 9 this morning. It says there are two fixes: a quick retry that would take about 40 minutes to clear the backlog, or a proper bulk send that needs about 40 lines of new code. It says re-running now is safe, because the provider ignores an invoice it has already seen. Which one do you want, the quick retry tonight or the proper bulk fix? Why did it break now?

It used to be fine because only a handful of invoices went out each night, well under the provider's limit. This month the new annual plans landed all at once, so the first night after that had thousands of invoices instead of dozens, and the job could not keep up. Nothing about the job changed. Its workload did. Which fix do you want, the quick retry or the proper bulk send? Options: Quick retry now, clears the backlog in about 40 minutes; Write the proper bulk fix first.

Say a normal night had about ninety invoices. The job sent them one at a time and stayed under the provider's hundred-a-minute limit, so everything went out fine. Then the first of the month arrives with four thousand two hundred, and the job sends them just as fast. The first hundred get through, and every one after that is turned away. Which fix do you want, the quick retry or the proper bulk send? Options: Quick retry now, clears the backlog in about 40 minutes; Write the proper bulk fix first.
More detail please.

Here is all of it. The job sends one request per invoice to the payment provider. Last night it had four thousand two hundred invoices, and the provider only accepts a hundred requests a minute. The first hundred went through, and the remaining four thousand one hundred came back refused. The job has no retry, so those four thousand one hundred were simply never sent, and those customers will get their invoice a day late unless the job runs again before nine this morning. transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

bench-codex found the flaky checkout test fails about one run in twelve, and it is the test's fault, not the app's. The test asks for a price before the app's cache has finished warming up, so it sometimes gets the undiscounted total. Nothing has been changed yet. Shall I have it fix the test the small recommended way? Options: Wait for the warm-up in the test setup, the three-line fix it recommends; Swap the cache for a stand-in in this test.
Then?

The rest of what it found is the cost: this flake has already blocked two releases, one Tuesday and one Thursday, and each time someone had to re-run the check by hand and wait about twenty-five minutes. That is why it is worth tidying. Nothing new has happened since I last looked, and it still has not touched any code. Shall I have it apply the small fix it recommends? Options: Wait for the price list to be ready in the test, the small fix it recommends; Swap in a stand-in price list for this test only.
More detail please.

What is left is how it checked: it ran that test many times over, and it failed seven of eighty-four runs, each time returning the full price of a hundred instead of the member price of eighty-five. Its two options differ in honesty rather than in size. The first is a few lines in the test setup, waiting for the price list to be ready, which it recommends. The second swaps in a stand-in price list for this one test, which is more code and would hide the very warm-up path that caused the trouble. That is everything it reported, and it has still changed nothing. Shall I have it apply the first fix and run that test a good many times to prove it holds? Options: Apply the small fix and re-run the test many times; Swap in the stand-in price list instead.
Why does that happen?

The test starts ordering before the app has finished loading its price list. If loading is quick, everything is fine. If it is slow, the test sees the plain prices instead of the member ones, and that is when it fails. Nothing is wrong with the app itself, only with the test being impatient. Clearer?
Give me an example.

Say it runs the checkout check twice in a row on the same code with nothing changed in between. The first time the price list loads in time and the total comes back at the member price, so it passes. The second time the price list is a moment slower, the total comes back at the full price, and the same check fails. Same code, same test, opposite answers, and the only difference is timing. Clearer?

transcript.text: What did bench-codex find about the flaky test? Explain it to me.

Codex found the cause of the flaky test. It sends its request before the price cache finishes warming up, so roughly one run in twelve reads stale prices and misses the member discount, which makes the check fail. It is a test problem, not a production bug, and it has not changed anything yet. It also says the flake blocked two deploys last week. Shall I have it apply the fix it recommends? Options: Apply the recommended fix; Leave it for now.
Then?

Codex offered two ways to fix it. It would rather have the test wait until the price cache is ready before it asks for prices, a three-line change. Its other idea is to put a stand-in cache in the test instead, which needs more work and hides the warm-up step. It has not touched anything yet, so it is waiting on your go-ahead. Shall I tell it to do the small one, the wait-until-ready fix? Options: Do the wait-until-ready fix; Do the stand-in cache fix; Leave it for now.
More detail please.

That is everything Codex found. The test failed seven times out of eighty-four runs this week. When it failed, the member price came out unrounded at full price instead of the discounted one, so the check saw a wrong total. The two blocked deploys each cost about twenty-five minutes of manual re-run, on Tuesday and Thursday. Two things it did not tell us: whether the rate is rising, and whether waiting for the cache makes the test slower. Shall I tell it to do the small wait-until-ready fix? Options: Do the wait-until-ready fix; Do the stand-in cache fix; Leave it for now.
Why does that happen?

Because the test and the price cache start at the same moment and the test does not wait. If the request arrives before the cache has finished filling, the checkout reads an empty cache and uses the plain price list, so the member price is never applied. It only goes wrong when the request wins that race, which is why the same test passes most runs and fails about one in twelve. Why the timing goes one way or the other varies run to run, and Codex did not say more than that. Shall I tell it to do the small wait-until-ready fix? Options: Do the wait-until-ready fix; Do the stand-in cache fix; Leave it for now.
Give me an example.

Here is one failing run from the record. A member's order comes to one hundred before discount, so the test expects eighty-five and the run printed a hundred instead. What happened in that run: the test sent the request immediately, the cache was still filling, so the checkout found no member price and charged the plain hundred. In the runs that pass, the cache was already full when the request landed, so the member price was there and the total came out at eighty-five. Shall I tell it to do the small wait-until-ready fix? Options: Do the wait-until-ready fix; Do the stand-in cache fix; Leave it for now.

verdicts.name: right_agent
verdicts.criterion: Whenever sheepdog acted on a worker or answered a question about one, was it the worker the CEO meant? verdicts.name: no_hallucination
verdicts.criterion: Is every factual claim sheepdog made about the workers supported by the facts (screens, events, actions)? verdicts.name: facts_current
verdicts.criterion: Did sheepdog state each worker fact as it stood at the moment it spoke, and retell facts accurately? Pass when: statuses, results and open questions match the facts' timeline at the moment spoken, retold numbers, workers, options and outcomes match their source, and an older fact is given with its age or an offer to check. Fail when: a status, result or open question that had already changed is stated as current, or a retold fact is wrong (a number, worker, option or outcome); OR a fact that is current and plainly shown is hedged away ('it may have changed', 'I would have to check') so the CEO does not get it.

verdicts.name: length_fits

Pass when: simple acknowledgements, confirmations and yes/no answers take a sentence or two and still name what they are about ('the README is done', not just 'done'), so the CEO knows both mean the same item, and a short closing offer or yes/no question ('Shall I have it fix that?') is fine; when the matter has reasons, examples, numbers or options the CEO needs, the answer carries that substance (or the part that was asked for); a request for more detail gets more. verdicts.name: ear_friendly

Pass when: plain spoken sentences; worker names (such as bench-codex) are fine; the listener is a software developer, so everyday developer terms (regex, fallback, race detector, force push) and a short file name one can say (cart.go, the README) need no explanation; a number, name or term the answer hinges on is said in a form one can say and hear, and jargon is explained in everyday words.
